en: Dīgha Nikāya 32 Āṭānāṭiyasutta 1. First Recitation Section Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four great kings. What four? The Great King Vessavaṇa, the lord of the Guhyakas; the Great King Dhatarattha, the lord of the Gandhabbas; the Great King Virūḷhaka, the lord of the Kumbhaṇḍas; and the Great King Virūpakkha, the lord of the Nāgas. These four great kings, bhikkhus, each have four sons. What four? Of the Great King Vessavaṇa, the lord of the Guhyakas, there are these four sons: Veṇudesa, Veṇu-dhāja, Gopāla, and Saṇāmika. Of the Great King Dhatarattha, the lord of the Gandhabbas, there are these four sons: Aṭṭhaka, Aṅkura, Soma, and Yama. Of the Great King Virūḷhaka, the lord of the Kumbhaṇḍas, there are these four sons: Dhaja, Upadhaja, Puṇṇa, and Vasu. Of the Great King Virūpakkha, the lord of the Nāgas, there are these four sons: Erāvaṇa, Cakkhupatha, Saṇṭhita, and Ghata. These sixteen great beings, bhikkhus, are the sons of the four great kings.

They dwell in their respective abodes, surrounded by their retinues, and they protect the four great continents together with the two intermediate islands. Now, bhikkhus, when the moon is full on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, the four great kings emerge from their respective abodes and go to the Sudhamma Hall in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Seated there, they survey the world-system with its four great continents and two intermediate islands. Then, bhikkhus, the Great King Vessavaṇa, the lord of the Guhyakas, surveys the eastern quarter. He sees those beings who are endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Seeing them, he is pleased and says: ‘It is well that such beings exist in the world! Then, bhikkhus, the Great King Dhatarattha, the lord of the Gandhabbas, surveys the southern quarter. He sees those beings who are endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Seeing them, he is pleased and says: ‘It is well that such beings exist in the world! Then, bhikkhus, the Great King Virūḷhaka, the lord of the Kumbhaṇḍas, surveys the western quarter. He sees those beings who are endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Seeing them, he is pleased and says: ‘It is well that such beings exist in the world! Then, bhikkhus, the Great King Virūpakkha, the lord of the Nāgas, surveys the northern quarter. He sees those beings who are endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Seeing them, he is pleased and says: ‘It is well that such beings exist in the world! When the moon is full on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, bhikkhus, the four great kings emerge from their respective abodes and go to the Sudhamma Hall in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Seated there, they survey the world-system with its four great continents and two intermediate islands. Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, approaches the four great kings and asks: ‘Have you, sirs, seen those beings who are endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom? ‘We have seen them, lord,’ they reply. ‘It is well that such beings exist in the world! It is well that such beings exist in the world! Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, approaches Sineru, the king of mountains, which is eighty-four thousand yojanas high, and ascends it. Having ascended, he surveys the world-system with its four great continents and two intermediate islands. Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, surveys the eastern quarter. He sees those beings who are endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Seeing them, he is pleased and says: ‘It is well that such beings exist in the world! Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, surveys the southern quarter... the western quarter... and the northern quarter. He sees those beings who are endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Seeing them, he is pleased and says: ‘It is well that such beings exist in the world! When the moon is full on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, approaches Sineru, the king of mountains, which is eighty-four thousand yojanas high, and ascends it. Having ascended, he surveys the world-system with its four great continents and two intermediate islands. Then, bhikkhus, Brahmā Sahampati approaches Sakka, lord of the devas, and says: ‘It is well, lord, that you have seen those beings who are endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. It is well that such beings exist in the world! It is well that such beings exist in the world! This, bhikkhus, is the first recitation section. [The second, third, and fourth recitation sections follow, detailing the protective verses of the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “Let the Great Kings and their retinues, And all the hosts of gods, protect this discourse. May the wise ones, having heard this spell, Live long and free from disease. [The protective verses continue... Thus have I heard. Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then the four Great Kings, together with a great army of yakkhas, a great army of gandhabbas, and a great...
Having stationed a guard in the four directions with a great army of kumbhaṇḍas and a great army of nāgas,
having stationed a troop in the four directions, and having established a defense in the four directions,
they approached the Blessed One at the end of the night, illuminating the entire Gijjhakūṭa mountain with their surpassing radiance; having approached, they...
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Some of those yakkhas, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side;
some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and having concluded the polite and courteous conversation, sat down to one side.
Some sat down; some, having extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One, sat down to one side;
some, having announced their name and clan, sat down to one side; and some, having become silent, sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the Great King Vessavaṇa said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, there are indeed powerful yakkhas who have no confidence in the Blessed One.
There are indeed, venerable sir, powerful yakkhas who have confidence in the Blessed One.
There are indeed, venerable sir, middling yakkhas who have no confidence in the Blessed One.”
For there are, venerable sir, middling yakkhas who are confident in the Blessed One;
there are, venerable sir, low yakkhas who are not confident in the Blessed One;
and there are, venerable sir, low yakkhas who are confident in the Blessed One.
"Moreover, venerable sir, for the most part the yakkhas have no faith in the Blessed One.
And why is that? Because, venerable sir, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the abstention from taking life; he teaches the Dhamma for the abstention from taking what is not given."
He teaches the Dhamma for abstaining from sexual misconduct; he teaches the Dhamma for abstaining from false speech;
he teaches the Dhamma for abstaining from fermented and distilled liquors, which are the basis for negligence.
Yet, Bhante, for the most part, the yakkhas are indeed unrestrained in the taking of life and unrestrained in the taking of what is not given.
They are unrestrained in sexual misconduct, unrestrained in false speech, and unrestrained in the use of fermented and distilled liquors, which are the basis for negligence.
That is unpleasant and disagreeable to them.

For there are, venerable sir, disciples of the Blessed One who resort to remote lodgings in forest thickets and jungle retreats—places that are quiet, with little noise, secluded from people, private from men, and suitable for seclusion.
"In that place there dwell powerful yakkhas who have no faith in this teaching of the Blessed One.

For their inspiration, may the Blessed One, venerable sir, learn the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the guarding, protection, non-harming, and comfortable dwelling of the bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the Great King Vessavaṇa, having understood the Blessed One’s consent, at that time recited this Āṭānāṭiya protection:
“Homage be to Vipassī,
the glorious one possessed of vision;”
And homage be to Sikhī,
who has compassion for all beings;
and homage be to Vessabhū.
To the one who has bathed, the ascetic;
homage be to Kakusandha,
the crusher of Māra’s army.
Homage be to Koṇāgamana,
the brahmin of perfected conduct;
and homage be to Kassapa.
To him who is completely liberated in every respect—
to the illustrious Aṅgīrasa,
the Son of the Sakyas— homage be!
He who taught this Dhamma,
which dispels all suffering,
and those who have attained Nibbāna in the world—
They saw things as they truly are;
those people were free from backbiting,
great, and devoid of fear.
It is for the welfare of gods and humans that they pay homage to Gotama,
who is perfected in true knowledge and conduct.
Great and free from timidity.
From where the sun rises—
the great, orb-bearing Ādicca—
For whom, as the sun is rising,
the night also ceases; for whom,
when the sun has risen—
‘The day’ is what it is called.
There too is a deep lake,
the ocean with its flowing waters.
Thus they know it there:
"The ocean has flowing water.
From here, that is the eastern direction.
Thus people describe him:
"That illustrious Great King protects this direction."
The lord of the gandhabbas,
known by the name Dhatarattha,
delights in dancing and singing.
Honored by the Gandhabbas,
he had many sons who all bore the same name; so have I heard.
Eighty, ten, and one,
all named Indra and possessed of great strength—
having seen the Buddha, they too...
To the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
they pay homage from afar—
to him who is great and free from timidity.
Homage to you, O noble steed among men;
homage to you, O supreme among men;
with skillful wisdom you behold.
Even non-human beings pay homage to him;
this has been heard by us repeatedly,
therefore we speak thus.
"Worship the Jina Gotama!
"We worship the Jina Gotama;
he who is perfected in true knowledge and conduct."
We pay homage to Gotama the Buddha—
by whom those called "petas," the malicious backbiters, are described.
Those who take life, the cruel,
thieves, and people of many guiles—
[thinking] "this is the southern direction from here," [they go].
Thus do people describe him:
"That glorious Great King protects this quarter."
The lord of the kumbhaṇḍas,
known by the name Virūḷha,
delights in dancing and singing.
Surrounded by kumbhaṇḍas,
he had many sons who,
I have heard, all bore the same name.
Eighty, ten, and one,
all named Indra and possessed of great strength;
they too, having seen the Buddha, [paid homage].
To the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
they pay homage from afar—
to him who is great and free from timidity.
Homage to you, O noble steed among men!
Homage to you, O supreme among men!
You behold with skillful wisdom.
Even non-human beings pay homage to him;
this has been heard by us repeatedly,
and therefore we speak thus.
“Worship the Jina Gotama!
“We worship the Jina Gotama,
who is perfected in true knowledge and conduct.”
We pay homage to the Buddha Gotama.
Wherever the sun goes—
the great Ādicca with his orb— there we go.
For whom, while the sun is setting,
even the day ceases; for whom,
when the sun has set—
‘Saṃvarī’ is what it is called.
There too is a deep lake,
the ocean with its flowing waters.
Thus they know it there as ‘the ocean with flowing waters’;
from here it is ‘the western direction.’
Thus people describe him:
"That glorious Great King protects whichever direction he oversees."
The lord of the nāgas,
known by the name Virūpakkha,
delights in dance and song.
Honored as if by the Nāgas themselves;
I have heard that he had many sons who all bore the same name.
Eighty, ten, and one,
all named Indra and possessed of great strength;
they too, having seen the Buddha, [paid homage].
To the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
they pay homage from afar—
to him who is great and free from timidity.
Homage to you, O noble steed among men;
homage to you, O supreme among men;
with skillful wisdom, you behold all.
Even non-human beings pay homage to him;
we have heard this repeatedly,
and therefore we speak thus.
"Pay homage to the Jina Gotama!
"We pay homage to the Jina Gotama,
who is perfected in true knowledge and conduct."
We pay homage to Buddha Gotama.
There where Uttarakuru is,
and the beautiful Mahāmeru;
Humans are born there,
free from the sense of "mine" and without possessions; they do not sow seeds.
Nor are plows led about;
humans enjoy rice that ripens without being tilled.
Having cooked fragrant rice-grains— free from husks, free from powder,
and pure— in a cauldron,
Then they eat their meal;
having made the cow one-hoofed,
they follow it in every direction.
Having made a single-hoofed animal their mount,
they roam from region to region;
or having made a woman their vehicle, [they travel].
They follow him from place to place;
having made a man their vehicle,
they follow him from place to place.
Having made a maiden their vehicle,
they wander from place to place;
having made a youth their vehicle, they wander from place to place.
They follow after [him] from region to region.
Having mounted their vehicles,
they travel all around in every direction.
There were vehicles for that king:
elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles,
and celestial vehicles were provided.
There were palaces and palanquins for the illustrious Great King,
and he had cities as well.
Well-established in the sky are the Āṭānāṭās,
the Kusināṭās, the Parakusināṭās,
the Nāṭasuriyās, and the Parakusiṭanāṭās.
To the north is Kasivanta,
and to the west is Janogha;
there are ninety-nine Ambarāmba-rativis.
The royal capital is named Āḷakamandā.
Furthermore, dear sir,
the royal capital of the Great King Kuvera is named Visāṇā.
Therefore the Great King Kuvera is called "Vessavaṇa. While dwelling in seclusion,
he makes things manifest.
Tatolā, tattalā, tatotalā;
Ojasi, tejasi, tatojasī;
Sūra, rājā, ariṭṭha, nemi.
There is also a lake there called Dharaṇī,
from which the clouds rain down,
and from which the rains spread forth.
There is also a hall there named Sālavatī,
where the yakkhas attend upon him;
there the trees bear fruit perpetually.
It was joined by various flocks of birds,
resounding with the cries of peacocks and herons,
and the sweet songs of cuckoos and other warblers.
Here there are the sounds of the jīvañjīvaka birds,
as well as those of the oṭṭhavacittaka,
the kukkuṭaka, and the kuḷīraka.
In the forest of Pokkharasāta,
there were the sounds of parrots and mynas,
as well as those of young brahmin students.
That Kuvera-lotus pond always shines at all times;
this is the northern direction from here.
Thus do people describe him:
"That glorious Great King protects this quarter."
The lord of the yakkhas,
known by the name Kuvera,
delights in dancing and singing.
Honored by the yakkhas themselves;
I have heard that he had many sons who all bore the same name.
Eighty, ten, and one,
all named Indra and possessed of great strength—
having seen the Buddha, they too...
To the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
they pay homage from afar—
to him who is great and free from fear.
Homage to you, O noble steed among men;
homage to you, O supreme among men;
with skill you have beheld.
Even non-human beings pay homage to him;
we have heard this repeatedly,
and therefore we speak thus.
"Worship the Jina Gotama!
"We worship the Jina Gotama,
who is perfected in true knowledge and conduct."
“We pay homage to the Buddha Gotama.
This, dear sir, is that Āṭānāṭiya protection for the safeguarding, protection, non-harming, and comfortable dwelling of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.
Whoever—whether a monk, a nun, a layman, or a laywoman—has properly grasped this Āṭānāṭiya protection, mastered it, and fully learned it, [they shall be safe].
If it is a non-human being— a male *yakkha*, a female *yakkhinī*, a male *yakkha*-child, a female *yakkha*-child, a high-ranking *yakkha* official,
a member of the *yakkha* assembly, or a servant of the *yakkhas*; or a *gandhabba*, a female *gandhabbī*,
a male *gandhabba*-child, a female *gandhabba*-child, a high-ranking *gandhabba* official, a member of the *gandhabba* assembly, or a servant of the *gandhabbas*.
or a kumbhaṇḍa, or a kumbhaṇḍī, or a kumbhaṇḍa youth, or a kumbhaṇḍa maiden, or a high minister of the kumbhaṇḍas, or an attendant of the kumbhaṇḍas,
or a follower of the kumbhaṇḍas; or a nāga, or a nāgī, or a nāga youth, or a nāga maiden, or a high minister of the nāgas,
or an attendant of the nāgas, or a follower of the nāgas— with a malicious mind [approaches] a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī...
Or if he were to follow a lay follower, male or female, when they are walking, or stand near them when they are standing,
or sit near them when they are sitting, or lie down near them when they are lying down— then, dear sir,
that non-human being would not receive honor or respect in villages or market towns.
“Good sir, that non-human being would not obtain a site or a dwelling in my royal capital named Āḷakamandā.
Good sir, that non-human being would not be allowed to go to the assembly of the *yakkhas*.
Furthermore, good sir, the non-humans would make it impossible for him to marry or to have his daughter married.”
Moreover, dear sir, non-human beings might even revile him with full-blown insults.
Moreover, dear sir, non-human beings might even turn his empty bowl upside down over his head.
Moreover, dear sir, non-human beings might even split his head into seven pieces.

For there are, dear sir, non-human beings who are fierce, cruel, and impetuous; they do not seize the Great Kings, nor do they seize the men of the Great Kings, nor do they seize the men of the men of the Great Kings.
These non-human beings, dear sir, are called "those who have obstructed the Great Kings.
Just as, dear sir, there might be great thieves in the realm of the King of Magadha.
They do not seize the King of Māgadha, nor do they seize the King of Māgadha’s men, nor do they seize the men of the King of Māgadha’s men.
Indeed, dear sir, those great thieves are called "those who have rebelled against the King of Māgadha.

In the same way, dear sir, there are non-human beings who are fierce, violent, and impetuous; they do not seize the Great Kings, nor do they seize the Great Kings’ men, nor do they seize the men of the Great Kings’ men.
Those non-human beings, dear sir, are called "those who have rebelled against the Great Kings.
For any non-human being, dear sir— whether it be a male *yakkha* or female *yakkhinī*, or a male *gandhabba* or female *gandhabbī*,

or a male *kumbhaṇḍa* or female *kumbhaṇḍī*, or a male *nāga* or female *nāgī*, or a male *nāga*-child or female *nāga*-child, or a high-ranking *nāga* official— [who has done so, they are called those who have rebelled].
Or a retainer of the nāgas, or a follower of the nāgas, with a malicious mind might follow a monk, a nun, a layman, or a laywoman as they walk;
or stand near them when they stand; or sit near them when they sit;
or lie down near them when they lie down.
One should complain, cry out, and wail against these yakkhas, great yakkhas, generals, and great generals:
“This yakkha seizes me! This yakkha possesses me! This yakkha harasses me! This yakkha oppresses me! This yakkha injures me! This yakkha harms me! This yakkha will not let me go!
Against which yakkhas, great yakkhas, generals, and great generals?
Inda, Soma, and Varuṇa,
Bhāradvāja, Pajāpati,
Candana, and Kāmaseṭṭha—
Kinnughaṇḍu and Nighaṇḍu,
Panāda and Opamañña,
and Mātali, the charioteer of the gods.
The gandhabba Cittasena,
King Nala Janesabha,
Sātāgira, and Hemavata.
Puṇṇaka, Karatiya, Guḷa; Sivaka, Mucalinda,
Vessāmitta, and Yugandhara.
Gopāla and Supparodha,
Hiri, Netti, and Mandiya;
Pañcālacaṇḍa and Āḷavaka.
Pajjunna, Sumana, Sumukha;
Dadhimukha, Maṇi, Māṇivara, Dīgha,
and also Serīsaka together.
To these yakkhas, great yakkhas, generals, and great generals, one should cry out, lament, and shout:
“This yakkha seizes! This yakkha enters! This yakkha afflicts! This yakkha torments! This yakkha harms! This yakkha injures! This yakkha does not let go!
This, dear sir, is the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the safeguarding, protection, non-injury, and comfortable dwelling of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.
“Now then, dear sir, we must go; we have many duties and much to do.
“Do as you think fit, great kings,” [the Blessed One replied].
Then the four Great Kings rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him with their right side toward him, and vanished right there.
Then some of those yakkhas rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to their right, vanished on the spot.
Some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and having concluded the polite and courteous conversation, vanished on the spot.
Some extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One and vanished on the spot.
Some, having announced their name and clan, vanished right there; some, having become silent, vanished right there.
The first recitation section is finished.
2. The second recitation section.
Then, when that night had passed, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, last night the Four Great Kings, having established protection in the four directions with a great army of yakkhas, a great army of gandhabbas,
a great army of kumbhaṇḍas, and a great army of nāgas, [stood watch] in the four directions."
Having established a guard around the monastery and set up a perimeter on all four sides, they approached me at the end of the night,
illuminating the entire Vulture Peak Mountain with their exquisite radiance.
Having approached and paid homage to me, they sat down to one side.
"Monks, some of those yakkhas, having approached me, paid homage and sat down to one side.
Some exchanged greetings with me, and after exchanging polite and courteous conversation, sat down to one side.
Some, raising their joined palms toward where I was, sat down to one side. Some [announced] their name and clan..."
Having announced themselves, some sat down to one side; some sat down to one side in silence.
Seated to one side, monks, the Great King Vessavaṇa said this to me:
“For there are, venerable sir, lofty yakkhas who are disbelievers toward the Blessed One... [and so on] ...there are, venerable sir, lowly yakkhas who are believers toward the Blessed One.”
"Moreover, venerable sir, for the most part the yakkhas have no faith in the Blessed One.

And why is that? Because, venerable sir, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the abstention from taking life... he teaches the Dhamma for the abstention from the use of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence."
"Moreover, Bhante, for the most part, yakkhas are indeed unrestrained in the taking of life... they are unrestrained in the use of liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness.
That is unpleasant and disagreeable to them.

For there are, Bhante, disciples of the Blessed One who resort to remote forest lodgings and jungle-thicket dwellings—places that are quiet, with little noise, secluded from people, private from men, and suitable for retreat."
"In that place there dwell powerful yakkhas who have no faith in this teaching of the Blessed One;
for their inspiration, may the Blessed One, venerable sir, learn the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the guarding,
protection, non-harming, and comfortable dwelling of the bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās."
“Monks, I consented by remaining silent.
Then, monks, the Great King Vessavaṇa, understanding my consent, at that time recited this Āṭānāṭiya protection:
‘May there be homage to Vipassī!’”
And let there be homage to the illustrious Cakkhumant, and also to Sikhī,
who has compassion for all beings.
And homage be to Vessabhu,
the one who has bathed away defilements, the ascetic;
homage be to Kakusandha.
Homage be to Koṇāgamana, the crusher of Māra’s army,
the Brahmin of perfected conduct.
Homage be to Kassapa,
who is completely liberated in every respect;
homage be to Aṅgīrasa.
Of the glorious son of the Sakyas,
who taught this Dhamma that dispels all suffering.
And those who have attained extinguishment in the world,
who have seen things as they truly are—
those people are free from backbiting.
Great ones, free from craving,
who bring welfare to gods and humans—
those who revere Gotama.
One endowed with true knowledge and conduct,
great and free from timidity—
from whom the sun rises.
The sun is a great orb; as it rises,
even the night ceases.
When the sun has risen,
it is called "day";
even a lake there is deep.
The ocean has flowing water;
thus they know it there as "the ocean with flowing water."

the direction which he protects.
He is a great king of renown,
the sovereign of the gandhabbas,
known by the name Dhatarattha.
Ramatī, preceded by Gandhabbas with dance and song;
he also had many sons.
Thus have I heard:
there were eighty-one of great strength, all named Indra.

the Buddha who is the Kinsman of the Sun,

we worship the Victor Gotama."

by whom the departed are proclaimed.
Slanderous backbiters,
those who take life, the cruel,
thieves, and people of many guiles.
"This is the southern direction," so people declare it;
the direction that he protects.
He is the illustrious great king,
the sovereign of the kumbhaṇḍas,
known by the name Virūḷha.

and where the sun goes to set.
The sun is a great orb;
when it sets, even the day comes to an end.
When the sun has risen,
it is called "the night";
even there, a lake may be deep.
The ocean has water that flows from rivers;
thus they know it there as "the ocean has water that flows from rivers."

the direction which he protects.
He is a great king of wide renown,
the sovereign of the nāgas,
known by the name Virūpakkha.
Ramatī, preceded by dancing and singing,
like one honored by Nāgas;
he also had many sons.

To where the Northern Kurus are—
Great Sineru is beautiful to behold;
there humans are born,
free from "mine-ness" and without possessions.
They do not sow seed,
nor are plows led forth;
the rice ripens without being tilled.
Human beings enjoy rice that is free from husks and powder, pure,
fragrant, and the fruit of the paddy plant.
Having cooked [the flesh] on a spit,
they eat their meal from it;
having turned a cow into a one-hoofed animal...
They follow [the caravan] from place to place;
having made a single-hoofed animal their guide,
they follow from place to place.
Having made a woman their vehicle,
they wander from place to place;
or having made a man their vehicle, [they wander from place to place].
They follow along from place to place.
Having made a young maiden their vehicle,
they follow along from place to place.
Having made the prince their vehicle,
they follow him in every direction;
having mounted those vehicles, they go forth.
They travel all around every direction as attendants of that king,
with elephant-vehicles and horse-vehicles.
A divine vehicle appeared,
as did palaces and palanquins for the illustrious Great King.
And his cities were well-established in the sky:
Āṭānāṭā, Kusināṭā, and Parakusināṭā.
Nāṭasuriyā and Parakusiṭanāṭā;
to the north, Kasivanta,
and to the west, Janogha.
There are ninety-nine [cities], Ambara and Ambaravati;
the royal capital named Āḷakamandā belongs to Kuvera, dear sir.
The royal capital of the Great King is named Visāṇā;
therefore, the Great King Kuvera is called "Vessavaṇa."
Paccesantā, Pakāsenti,
Tatolā, Tattalā, Tatotalā,
Ojasi, Tejasi, Tatojasī.
King Sūra, Ariṭṭha, and Nemi;
and there too is the lake named Dharaṇī,
from which the clouds pour forth rain.
Where the rains burst forth,
there is a hall named Sālavatī,
where the yakkhas pay their respects.
There, the trees bear fruit perpetually;
they are frequented by various flocks of birds,
resounding with the cries of peacocks and cranes.
With the sweet songs of the cuckoo and others,
with the cries of the jīvañjīvaka birds here,
and likewise with the calls of the oṭṭhavacittaka;
Cocks and quails,
and lotus-herons in the forest; there,
parrots and mynas raise their cries.
And the Daṇḍamāṇavaka [ponds];
that Kuvera’s lotus-lake always shines at all times.
"This is the northern direction," so people declare it—
referring to that direction which he protects.

the sovereign of the yakkhas,
known by the name Kuvera.

he also had many sons.

“We pay homage to the Buddha Gotama, who is perfect in true knowledge and conduct.
This, dear sir, is the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the protection, guarding, safety, and comfortable dwelling of the bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Whosoever, dear sir— whether a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a layman, or a laywoman—
shall have this Āṭānāṭiya protection well-learned, mastered, and fully acquired, if a non-human being—

a male yakkha or a female yakkha …pe… a male gandhabba or a female gandhabba …pe… a male kumbhaṇḍa or a female kumbhaṇḍa …pe… or a male nāga [should approach them]... [text continues] ...he shall not be able to harm them."
Or a female nāga, or a young male nāga, or a young female nāga, or a high-ranking nāga official,
or a nāga attendant, or a nāga follower— should one with a malicious mind follow a monk, a nun, a layman, or a laywoman as they walk,
or stand beside them when they are standing, or sit near them when they are sitting, or lie down beside them when they are lying down.
“Good sir, that non-human being would not receive honor or respect in my villages or market towns.
Good sir, that non-human being would not obtain a site or a dwelling in the royal capital named Āḷakamandā.
Good sir, that non-human being would not be permitted to go to the assembly of the *yakkhas*.”
Moreover, dear sir, non-human beings might make him unapproachable and inaccessible.
Moreover, dear sir, non-human beings might revile him with full-blown insults.
Moreover, dear sir, non-human beings might even turn their empty bowl upside down over his head.
Moreover, dear sir, non-human beings might even split his head into seven pieces.

For there are, dear sir, non-human beings who are fierce, cruel, and impetuous; they do not seize the Great Kings, nor do they seize the attendants of the Great Kings, nor do they seize the attendants of the attendants of the Great Kings.
These, dear sir, are called the non-human beings who have taken possession of the Great Kings.

"Just as, dear sir, there might be great thieves in the realm of the King of Magadha who do not seize anything from the King of Magadha himself, nor from the King’s men, nor even from the men of the King’s men;
those great thieves, dear sir, are called ‘those who have rebelled against the King of Magadha.’"

In the same way, dear sir, there are non-human beings who are fierce, violent, and impetuous; they do not seize the Great Kings, nor do they seize the attendants of the Great Kings, nor do they seize the attendants of the attendants of the Great Kings.
These, dear sir, are called the non-human beings who have taken possession of the Great Kings.
For any non-human being whatsoever—whether a male *yakkha* or a female *yakkhinī*, or a *gandhabba* or a *gandhabbī*—[who acts thus].
...pe... whether it be a kumbhaṇḍa or a kumbhaṇḍī ...pe... whether it be a nāga or a nāgī ...pe...

with a corrupt mind, [such a being] might approach a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī, a male lay follower or a female lay follower who is walking, or stand near one who is standing, or sit near one who is sitting, or lie down near one who is lying down.
One should complain, cry out, and wail against these yakkhas, great yakkhas, generals, and great generals:
“This yakkha seizes me! This yakkha possesses me! This yakkha harms me! This yakkha injures me! This yakkha strikes me! This yakkha afflicts me! This yakkha will not let me go!
Against which yakkhas, great yakkhas, generals, and great generals?
Inda, Soma, and Varuṇa,
Bhāradvāja, Pajāpati,
Candana, and Kāmaseṭṭha—
Kinnughaṇḍu and Nighaṇḍu,
Panāda and Opamañña,
and Mātali, the charioteer of the gods.
Cittasena the gandhabba,
Nala the king, Janesabha,
Sātāgira, and Hemavata.
Puṇṇaka, Karatiya, Guḷa; Sivaka, Mucalinda,
Vessāmitta, and Yugandhara.
Gopāla and Supparodha,
Hiri, Netti, and Mandiya;
Pañcālacaṇḍa and Āḷavaka.
Pajjunna, Sumana, Sumukha;
Dadhimukha, Maṇi, Māṇivara, Dīgha,
and also Serīsaka together.
To these *yakkhas*, great *yakkhas*, generals, and great generals, one should cry out, lament, and shout:
“This *yakkha* seizes! This *yakkha* possesses! This *yakkha* harms! This *yakkha* afflicts! This *yakkha* injures! This *yakkha* torments! This *yakkha* will not release!
This, dear sir, is the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the protection, guarding, non-harming, and comfortable dwelling of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.
“But now, dear sir, we must depart; we have many duties and much to do.
“Then, great kings, go at your own convenience,” I said.
Then, monks, the four Great Kings rose from their seats, paid homage to me, circumambulated me keeping me to their right, and vanished right there.
Then, bhikkhus, those yakkhas rose from their seats; some, having bowed down to me and kept me on their right, vanished right there.
Some exchanged greetings with me, and when they had concluded their polite and friendly conversation, they vanished right there.
Some, having extended their joined palms toward me, vanished right there.
Some, having announced their name and clan, vanished right there;
some, having become silent, vanished right there.
"Monks, learn the Āṭānāṭiya protection."
“Memorize, monks, the Āṭānāṭiya protection; master it, monks, the Āṭānāṭiya protection.
For the benefit of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, the Āṭānāṭiya protection is conducive to their guarding, protection, safety from harm, and dwelling in comfort.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Āṭānāṭiya Sutta, the ninth, is finished.
